comparator.name: Bestuurs- en organisatiewetenschap (Public Administration and Organisation Science)
comparator.sourceNotes: The 2026–2027 curriculum and regulations specify a 142.5 EC major and 37.5 EC of profiling, including a 22.5 EC graduation project. Profiling requires at least 15 EC at level 3. Students entering from September 2020 onward complete 15 EC in an international context across the degree. Qualitative Research requires both Introduction to Research and Quantitative Research; the graduation project requires Qualitative Research. The capstone requires Organisations in Transition and Policy, Rationality and Power. Unconditional entry to year three requires passing years one and two; exceptions require an examination-board decision. Overlapping profiling content can lead to a proportional credit reduction.

audience.programmeDescription: Utrecht’s Public Administration and Organisation Science degree studies how governments and organisations make decisions, deliver services and respond to societal problems. Students combine policy, law, sociology and management with quantitative and qualitative research, professional skills and an individual graduation project.
audience.comparisonExplanation: The broad UCR option connects public institutions, law and economics to policy analysis and sustainability governance. The second emphasises organisational behaviour, leadership and responsible strategy while retaining political, legal and empirical foundations. Utrecht offers a more integrated Dutch public-administration and public-service curriculum and requires a 22.5 EC individual graduation project.

curriculum.limitation: The outline preserves the 142.5 EC major and 37.5 EC of profiling. The degree is taught mainly in Dutch, with English study and an international-context requirement. Course entry and year-three progression remain subject to Utrecht’s regulations.

alternatives.label: Public governance, policy and organisations
alternatives.labelReason: The plan gives sustained attention to political institutions, public law, public economics and public problems, alongside organisational theory and empirical research.
alternatives.concept: Investigate how public institutions and organisations make policy and respond to societal problems. Combine comparative politics and public law with public economics, organisational research and stakeholder negotiation. Apply these perspectives to policy analysis and a sustainability governance problem.
progression: Research Methods and Statistics precedes the quantitative leadership survey. Introductory law precedes constitutional and international law; introductory politics precedes EU politics. Introductory economics supports later public economics and behavioural analysis.

alternatives.label: Public organisations, leadership and management
alternatives.labelReason: Organisational behaviour, leadership, communication and responsible strategy form a sustained direction, grounded in the programme’s interests in public responsibility and improving management. Business courses provide comparative organisational context.
alternatives.concept: Explore how organisations with public responsibilities are led, governed and changed. Combine organisational psychology, leadership communication and empirical research with political and legal institutions, public economics and responsible business strategy. Study public problems through conflict analysis and policy advice.
progression: Business Foundations precedes transnational business law, business governance and digital strategy. Research Methods and Statistics precedes the quantitative leadership survey. Introductory economics precedes public economics and behavioural analysis. Introductory politics and law support later institutional and public-problem analysis.
alternatives.distinctness: Six courses differ in each plan, representing 45 EC. This direction develops business governance, digital strategy and personal leadership, while the broad plan gives more room to public policy, international law, human rights, ethics and sustainability governance. Shared research, political, economic and organisational foundations keep both connected to the Utrecht degree.

trace: Introduces legal systems and legal reasoning, public and private law and socio-legal inquiry, providing foundations for later constitutional and international law.
Builds a sociological framework for inequality, social structure and networks, which can inform study of public organisations.
Introduces economic institutions, markets and public-policy trade-offs.
Develops research design, operationalisation, sampling and statistics for governance and organisational inquiry.
Develops interview, ethnographic, participatory and documentary methods, coding and reflexivity for social inquiry.
Develops leadership communication for aligning people and explaining organisational decisions.
Adds normative reasoning about responsibility, justice and contested public choices.
Provides comparative analysis of political institutions, electoral systems and public decision-making.
Introduces political thought and normative argument about authority, power and public responsibility.
Develops rhetorical analysis and persuasive public communication relevant to policy and leadership.
Examines rights and philosophical arguments that constrain and legitimate public action.
Compares constitutional limits, governmental powers and institutional rights protections.
Develops theory-driven hypotheses, psychological measures, an ethical original survey, statistical analysis and empirical reporting on leadership, belonging and inclusion.
Directly studies public goods, market failure, public spending and political economy.
Uses negotiation cases and strategic tools to examine stakeholder interests, bargaining, power, trust and trade-offs.
Studies EU institutions, decision rules and policy-making across levels of government.
Directly examines organisational behaviour, motivation, leadership, groups, culture and decision-making.
Uses social theory and empirical sources to investigate civil-society organisations, public spheres and social movements.
Examines persuasion, framing, nudging and their ethics in public and organisational communication.
Explains behavioural decision-making, incentives and externalities relevant to public policy.
Examines how actors, interests, public opinion and enforcement shape sustainability policy.
Examines phases of policymaking through a sugar case across national and international arenas, and develops policy memo writing.
Adds international legal institutions and treaty processes to the governance perspective.
Introduces organisations, value creation, stakeholders and management foundations.
Builds reflective personal leadership, collaboration and responsible professional agency.
Examines commercial contracts, cross-border regulation and dispute resolution as context for organisations working with businesses across jurisdictions.
Adds cross-border governance, corporate responsibility and institutional strategy.
Develops a strategic plan and analyses responsible digital transformation through company and industry cases; supplies a comparative private-sector perspective on organisational change.
Combines disciplinary perspectives on conflict and public responsibility in an evidence-based policy brief and research dossier; develops context, stakeholder and policy-option analysis.
blocks: Both compare political institutions and their consequences. UCR uses comparative political evidence; Utrecht places this in a required English-taught major course.
Both examine normative arguments about political authority and public responsibility. Their author selections and emphasis differ.
Both address constitutional institutions and administrative law, including participation and legal remedies. UCR compares jurisdictions; Utrecht develops Dutch constitutional and administrative law.
Both examine organisational structures, people, power and culture. UCR develops organisational psychology and evidence synthesis; Utrecht integrates four organisational frames and a simulation.

Both analyse organisational change and strategic responses. UCR studies responsible digital transformation through company cases; Utrecht examines organisational transitions in a broader public context.
Public policy, economics and societal problems

Both analyse public problems through governance frameworks, consult stakeholders or experts and develop policy advice. UCR applies this to a sustainability issue; Utrecht integrates the degree’s public-administration perspectives and a governance simulation.
Both study policy development and the assessment of policy choices. UCR applies policy analysis through a sugar-policy case; Utrecht gives explicit attention to rationality, power and a policy plan.

Both integrate perspectives on a public problem and formulate advice. UCR produces a conflict-related policy brief and evidence dossier; Utrecht integrates governance and organisational practice more broadly.
Both use sociological perspectives to analyse societal developments and public questions. UCR concentrates on civil society, public spheres and movements; Utrecht surveys changes in Dutch society.
Both develop research design, measurement and statistical reasoning. UCR provides general empirical methods that later courses apply to leadership and organisations.

Both use qualitative research design, interviews or observation and systematic analysis. Utrecht allocates 15 EC to commissioned organisational research; UCR supplies a 7.5 EC general qualitative methods course.

Both develop hypotheses, operationalise concepts, collect original survey data and analyse and report findings. UCR investigates leadership and inclusion; Utrecht researches an issue concerning public organisations.
Public-service specialisation, independent research and study choices

Utrecht introduces Dutch public administration, governance and public organisations in one integrated course. UCR develops related political, legal, economic and organisational perspectives across separate courses.
Utrecht has a dedicated course applying management concepts to public services, including an advisory case. UCR develops leadership, organisational psychology and strategy across separate courses.
Utrecht requires philosophy of science. UCR’s Ethics course addresses moral arguments and does not provide the same dedicated examination of scientific knowledge.
This 7.5 EC choice forms part of Utrecht’s profiling space.
Utrecht reserves another 30 EC for profiling choices.

Utrecht requires an individual 22.5 EC graduation project with preparation, empirical research and a thesis. UCR’s scheduled course projects and optional independent research have a different structure.

selection.assessment: Two directions respond to the programme’s seven direct interests: public governance and policy, and organisational leadership and management. Each has a complete 180 EC plan, substantive empirical research and advanced public-problem analysis. The second adds six different courses. Finance, methods and international institutions support these directions; the remaining illustrative examples and outcomes do not justify a third coherent interest-led programme.

notes.text: Utrecht combines public administration, organisation science and professional skills in a Dutch degree with a 22.5 EC individual graduation project. UCR connects these interests through comparative politics and law, economics, organisational research and applied public-problem analysis. Its optional independent research sits outside the scheduled 180 EC.

Utrecht gives dedicated attention to Dutch public administration, public-service management, philosophy of science and integrated organisational practice. UCR’s business and strategy courses offer comparative perspectives; they do not reproduce this public-service sequence or the required Utrecht thesis.
